headline: No public sign that Russia is preparing a conventional attack on the Baltic states. Hybrid pressure (sabotage, GPS jamming, drones and border provocations) remains high and active.
conventional_note: Nothing reported on troop massing, field hospitals or blood supplies moving toward Baltic borders. Estonia's intelligence service sees no intention to attack NATO this year; Danish and US intelligence see a low but growing risk of a limited test.
hybrid_note: Sabotage arrests in Germany, Poland and Romania this week, persistent GPS jamming around Kaliningrad, and armed escorts pushing migrants at the Latvia–Belarus border earlier this month.
changed: First edition, so there is no previous day to compare against. From tomorrow this section lists only what is new, rising or easing.
bottom_line: The gap between alarm and evidence is today's main story. The most-shared item, Reuters' report that the Pentagon asked the Baltic states to tone down their warnings about Russia, rests on four anonymous sources; dozens of outlets repeating it add reach, not corroboration. Meanwhile the physical signs that would come before a conventional attack are absent from public reporting. The realistic near-term risk is a deniable, limited incident (a drone, sabotage, a border provocation) rather than an invasion. Danish intelligence warned that Russia might blame weapons landing on NATO soil on Ukrainian jamming, which is worth keeping in mind when reading drone stories like the one in Lithuania on 18 October.

headline: Estonia refuses on the record to soften its warnings after the Pentagon report, and Lithuanian police tie Starlink arson attempts in three EU countries to one network. Still no public sign of preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Putin said on 29 October that Russia is ready for but does not want a war with Europe. The overnight blackout in Kaliningrad has an official technical explanation and no sign of military activity.
hybrid_note: Lithuania announced terrorism suspicions against two men linked to Starlink arson attempts in Lithuania, Bulgaria and Poland; Poland blames Russian intelligence. GPS jamming remains persistent. No new drone or border incident reported.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Incident counts: one sabotage case (the Starlink arson network, announced 27–29 October and not covered in yesterday's edition), zero in the other four metrics. New: Estonia's prime minister publicly rejected calls to tone down criticism of Russia, Peskov called Baltic rhetoric hysterically aggressive, Politico reported US pressure on Lithuania to let Belarusian potash through Klaipėda, and Kaliningrad had a region-wide blackout overnight.
bottom_line: The evidence still points to hybrid pressure, not preparation for invasion. The Starlink case is the most substantial new development: prosecutors in three countries have linked the attacks, and the Russian connection rests on a Polish minister's attribution and on reports that a Turkish gang's leader lives under Russian protection, while Lithuanian police say the motive is not yet established. The Pentagon story has moved from anonymous sourcing to on-the-record Baltic reactions, but those reactions disagree: Estonia's foreign minister says there was no official request, while its prime minister says allies are asking Estonia to hold back. Read together with the Politico potash report, the picture is US pressure on Baltic positions as part of a push for a deal with Moscow; both reports rely on anonymous European officials. The Kaliningrad blackout drew online speculation about sabotage, but nothing so far contradicts the authorities' explanation of a protection system tripping at a power plant. The Telegraph's report that Moscow will demand a NATO pullback to 1997 lines rests on unnamed diplomatic sources and is not confirmed by any official.

headline: A quiet 24 hours with no new airspace, border or sabotage incidents. Lithuania's defence minister and Estonia's prime minister say no US request to tone down warnings reached them, while Estonia and Latvia move to give border guards wider powers against crossings they say Minsk organises.
conventional_note: Still no reports of troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. ISW reports nothing significant on Russian military activity in Belarus. The only new exercise news is the concept for Union Shield 2027, a Russia–Belarus drill set for next year.
hybrid_note: No new drone, sabotage or border incident in the last day, but the pattern of recent weeks (the Starlink arson network, persistent GPS jamming, Belarus-organised migration) is unchanged. Poland charged a Russian national with spying after he was caught photographing railway infrastructure.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Incident counts: zero in all five metrics (yesterday one sabotage case). New: Lithuania's defence minister and Estonia's prime minister both said no US request to soften their language reached them, so the claim tracker moves the Pentagon story from Likely to Contested. Estonia's and Latvia's interior ministers proposed closing crossing points with Belarus for a while and widening border guards' powers to use force. Correction: yesterday's edition said Lithuania had not commented on the Pentagon report; its defence minister had said on 30 October that he had no information about such a request.
bottom_line: The evidence picture has not moved: hybrid pressure continues, and there is no public sign of preparation for a conventional attack. The Pentagon story now faces on-the-record statements from Lithuania and Estonia that no request reached them, but those statements deny only an official request, and Reuters described informal conversations, so the two accounts can both be true. The Estonian and Latvian moves on border force are a response to months of Belarus-organised crossings, not to a new incident, and closing crossings would be a political choice with costs for both sides. ISW says the Kremlin keeps demanding that NATO return to its 1997 footprint, but the primary statement behind that is not cited, so the Telegraph report of a formal demand in talks stays unconfirmed. Reports of men being seized off Russian streets to sign army contracts point to recruitment strain for the Ukraine war rather than a build-up aimed at the Baltics. A quiet day in public reporting is not proof of a quiet day on the ground, especially for the logistics and medical indicators.

headline: An unidentified object, probably a drone, entered eastern Latvia from the Russia–Belarus border area on Sunday evening and left after about 30 minutes; its origin is unknown. No other new incidents, and still no public sign of preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. NATO's top commander said on 30 October that conflict with Russia is not inevitable. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because Russia's forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: A new airspace incursion over Krāslava and Ludza in Latvia adds to a pattern of drones, sabotage, persistent GPS jamming and Belarus-organised migration. No new sabotage, jamming or border incident was first reported in the last day.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. The airspace indicator stays Elevated but its trend moves from Unchanged to Rising. Incident counts: one airspace incident (the object over eastern Latvia on 1 November; yesterday zero), zero in the other four metrics, as yesterday. Also new to the tracker: satellite imagery of a large over-the-horizon radar under construction near Gvardeysk in Kaliningrad, first reported on 21 October.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat and persistent hybrid pressure, with nothing suggesting Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic direction. The Latvian incursion is the only new incident, and the facts are thin: the armed forces have not said what the object was or where it came from. Past stray drones over Latvia have included both Ukrainian drones pushed off course, reportedly by Russian jamming, and Russian ones, so neither origin should be assumed; Izvestia's headline calls it a drone and links it to stories about Ukrainian drones, which runs ahead of the Latvian statement. The Kaliningrad radar, seen on commercial satellite imagery, fits the baseline's picture of Russia steadily building long-term military capacity, but it is a sensor, not a sign of imminent action, and it is not known to be operational. The debate in Estonia over whether its warnings about Russia have become too predictable is a political argument, not new evidence about Russian intentions. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland puts police on full readiness along the Kaliningrad border after intelligence warnings of possible Russian sabotage in the coming days. No new incidents were reported, and there is still no public sign of preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Poland's operation is a police response to a sabotage warning, not to troop movements. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Polish police and counter-terrorism units have reinforced the Kaliningrad border area from 2 to 8 November after warnings from military intelligence and allied services. Estonia deported a Russian citizen its security service links to Russian intelligence. GPS jamming, drones and Belarus-organised migration remain the background.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. The sabotage indicator stays High but its trend moves from Unchanged to Rising because of Poland's official sabotage alert; the airspace trend eases back from Rising to Unchanged as no new incursion was reported. Incident counts: zero in all five metrics (yesterday one airspace incident, the object over eastern Latvia). New: Poland's border operation and Estonia's deportation of a Russian citizen over intelligence contacts.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat and active hybrid pressure, with no sign that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The most important new item is Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border, which the national police chief confirmed on the record and tied to sabotage and the actions of eastern intelligence services. The more dramatic detail, that armed groups might try to cross from Kaliningrad, comes from anonymous sources quoted by the Polish broadcaster RMF and has not been confirmed by any named official; several outlets repeating RMF count as one source. A preventive alert is not evidence that an attack is coming, and authorities have reported no incident so far. Estonia's deportation fits the baseline's warnings about hostile intelligence activity, but the evidence behind it is not public. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland says it headed off a possible provocation on the Kaliningrad border, and Latvia now judges that one of two drones that entered its airspace was a Russian Geran. Neither event points to preparations for a conventional attack.
conventional_note: Still no reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains heading toward Baltic borders, and Lithuania's defence ministry has said its military intelligence sees no significant change in Kaliningrad. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Polish border guards saw people with flashlights near the Kaliningrad border shortly after midnight on 3 November, during an operation launched on intelligence warnings of sabotage and possible armed incursions. Latvia says a drone on 1 November was most likely a Russian Geran and a second on 3 November looked Ukrainian. GPS jamming and Belarus-organised migration remain the background.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: airspace moves from Unchanged to Rising (a new drone on 3 November and Latvia's attribution of the 1 November drone to Russia); border pressure moves from Unchanged to Rising (the Sępopol incident); sabotage goes back from Rising to Unchanged because no new warning or case was added. Incident counts: 1 airspace incident and 1 border incident (yesterday all zero); sabotage, GPS jamming and official threats stay at zero. New: Tusk's on-the-record account of the warnings, Germany's brigade in Lithuania stepping up electronic surveillance, and Russia's embassy in Warsaw calling the sabotage warnings fake.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat and active hybrid pressure, with no sign of Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The Sępopol incident is real but thin: border guards saw people with flashlights on the Russian side, nobody crossed, and Tusk himself said he could not be sure a provocation was intended. The stronger part of Poland's case is the warnings behind the operation, which Tusk now describes on the record as coming from Polish, NATO and, according to AP, also Ukrainian and US services; their evidence remains unpublished, and Moscow dismisses them as fake without offering any counter-evidence. Latvia's assessment that the 1 November drone was most likely a Russian Geran matters more than the coverage suggests, because it reverses the stray-Ukrainian-drone framing pushed by Russian state media, but it rests on tracking data, not wreckage. Many headlines describe a 'thwarted provocation' as if an attack was stopped; the evidence supports only a quick response to suspicious movement. The planned US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November are worth watching against the baseline, since a ceasefire is the main development that could eventually free Russian forces. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland's special-services coordinator warns that something 'very massive' could happen on both sides of the Kaliningrad border, staged to be blamed on Ukrainians, and Germany arrests a suspected organiser of the Starlink arson near Warsaw. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. A Lithuanian border-post commander describes the extra jet, helicopter and training-ground activity he sees as routine. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border continues amid on-the-record warnings of sabotage or provocations in the first half of November; the minister coordinating Poland's special services says the warnings are serious but imprecise. German prosecutors arrested a man suspected of ordering the 23 September arson at a Starlink ground station south of Warsaw, which Poland blames on Russian intelligence. GPS jamming and Belarus-organised migration remain the background.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: sabotage moves from Unchanged to Rising (a new arrest in the Starlink case and the Polish minister's warning of a large staged provocation); airspace and border pressure go back from Rising to Unchanged because no new drone or border incident was reported. Incident counts: 1 sabotage case (yesterday 0); airspace incidents and border incidents fall from 1 to 0; GPS jamming and official Russian threats stay at 0. New: the 'blame Ukrainians' warning from Poland's special-services coordinator, US European Command's force-protection campaign, and Lukashenko calling NATO an 'aggressive bloc' while insisting Minsk and Moscow will attack no one.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat, with active hybrid pressure aimed at Poland and the Baltic states and no sign that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The most important new element is Tomasz Siemoniak's on-the-record warning that a provocation could be staged to look Ukrainian; it fits a pattern the baseline describes (information operations and preparation for disruptive acts), but he himself called the intelligence imprecise, and no evidence has been published. The Starlink arrest is the strongest hard evidence of the day: prosecutors in Germany, Poland and Lithuania are building cases against a network that allegedly used hired criminals, though the link to Russian intelligence still rests on official allegations and press reporting rather than published proof. Russian state media present Poland's operation as a political distraction, but offer no evidence and ignore that NATO's top commander and several allied services shared the warnings. Coverage that treats the coming days, including Poland's Independence Day on 11 November, as a countdown to an attack goes beyond the evidence; heightened vigilance is justified, alarm is not. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November and the Pentagon's European troop options due around 6 November are the developments to watch against the baseline. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Lithuania expels three Ukrainians it says were tasked by hostile intelligence services, and Poland charges six people over supplying Russia's military, as Russia's Security Council chief accuses Poland and the Baltic states of training people to undermine Russia. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Counter-intelligence activity is intense across the region: Lithuania's State Security Department (VSD) had three Ukrainian citizens expelled for paid filming and information-gathering tasks received over Telegram, Poland's ABW detained six people accused of supplying Russia with weapons components, and a Romanian court ordered the arrest of a man living in Russia over a 2024 sabotage plot. Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border runs until at least 8 November, and a new OSINT map shows GPS interference along almost the whole eastern flank.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: official Russian rhetoric moves from Unchanged to Rising (Shoigu's accusation that Poland and the Baltic states train people to work against Russia, and Zakharova's reminder that Russia may answer with 'asymmetrical' measures); sabotage moves from Rising back to Unchanged (activity continues at the same pace). Incident counts: GPS jamming reports rise from 0 to 1 (an OSINT map of interference on 3 November); sabotage cases stay at 1 (a Romanian arrest order); airspace incidents, border incidents and official Russian threats stay at 0. New: the VSD expulsions and the Polish ABW espionage arrests.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat combined with active hybrid pressure, and nothing to suggest Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The strongest new facts are official ones: the VSD's expulsion of three people recruited online for paid reconnaissance-type tasks matches the baseline's warning about hostile services recruiting through messaging apps, and Poland's ABW arrests are backed by a court order. Both, however, rest on evidence that has not been made public, and the VSD did not say which country's services were involved, so 'Russia-linked' is an inference, not a published finding. Shoigu's claim that Poland and the Baltic states train people to destroy Russia from within offers no evidence and mirrors Western accusations back at the West; it is best read as narrative preparation, and possibly as justification for future 'asymmetrical' responses, rather than as a sign of military intent. Poland's warning window (the operation runs to at least 8 November, with Independence Day on 11 November) has so far passed without a confirmed incident, which neither proves the warnings wrong nor right. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November and any outcome of the Pentagon's Europe posture review, whose options were due around today, are the developments most likely to shift the baseline. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: A Finnish court jails a ship's captain and a senior officer over the New Year's Eve cable damage in the Gulf of Finland, Reuters reports Russian military satellites edging toward a second Finnish radar satellite, and NATO begins six weeks of German-led drills in Lithuania. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment, which judges the near-term conventional threat low because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: The Helsinki District Court convicted the captain and a senior officer of the cargo ship Fitburg of aggravated criminal damage for dragging an anchor across Finland–Estonia undersea cables, the kind of shadow-fleet incident the Lithuanian assessment warns about. Russian satellites keep shadowing commercial radar satellites run by Finland's ICEYE, which supplies imagery to Ukraine. Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border runs until at least 8 November, and ACLED counts 20 suspected Russian hybrid events in Poland so far this year.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged. Trends: official Russian rhetoric moves from Rising back to Unchanged (no new senior statement against NATO or the Baltic states found since yesterday). Incident counts: sabotage cases stay at 1 (the Helsinki court's verdict in the Fitburg cable case); GPS jamming reports fall from 1 to 0; airspace incidents, border incidents and official Russian threats stay at 0. New: the Fitburg convictions, Reuters' report on Russian satellites approaching a second ICEYE satellite, and the start of German-led NATO drills with more than 6,000 troops in Lithuania.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat, active hybrid pressure, and nothing to suggest Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction. The Fitburg verdict is the strongest new fact, because a court tested the evidence; but it found the crew guilty of criminal damage, not of acting for the Russian state, and a separate Finnish court dismissed charges in the Eagle S case in October, which shows how hard intent is to prove. The satellite story rests on public orbital data showing real and unusual manoeuvres, yet 'attack rehearsal' is one analyst's interpretation, Germany's space commander warns that capability is not proof of intent, and reported distances range from 26 metres to about a kilometre, so headlines run ahead of the evidence. US signals are mixed: Lithuania says two US battalions are heading to Pabradė while the Pentagon's Europe posture review is still pending and a Politico report, denied by Lithuania's foreign minister, says US officials raised Belarusian fertiliser transit through Klaipėda. Poland's warning window has so far passed without a confirmed incident. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November matter most for the baseline, since a ceasefire could in time free Russian forces. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: A gunman kills six people in Kraków's Main Square; Polish officials point to far-right views and have named no foreign link. Moscow says any Coalition of the Willing troops in Ukraine would be legitimate targets as the coalition's first drills open in Poland on 9 November. There is still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. ISW reports manpower shortages in a Russian army in eastern Ukraine and no redeployments toward NATO territory, which fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat because most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new sabotage, drone or border incident was first reported in the last day, but the pattern the Lithuanian assessment describes (shadow-fleet cable damage, GPS interference around Kaliningrad, hostile-intelligence recruitment) is unchanged. The Kraków shooting is a likely target for false online claims; Polish officials have so far given no sign of Russian involvement. Poland's operation on the Kaliningrad border was scheduled to run until at least 8 November with no confirmed crossing attempt.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged (17 of 39). Incident counts: official Russian threats rise from 0 to 1 (Zakharova's statement that Coalition of the Willing troops in Ukraine would be legitimate targets); sabotage cases fall from 1 to 0; airspace incidents, GPS jamming reports and border incidents stay at 0. New: the Kraków shooting (not linked to Russia by officials), Moscow's reaction to the KOALICJA 26.2 drills in Poland, and ISW's reading of Russia's team for the 10–11 November Abu Dhabi talks.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: a low near-term conventional threat, steady hybrid pressure, and nothing to suggest Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic direction; ISW in fact reports manpower strain on one Russian front. The Kraków shooting is the day's biggest news in the region, but so far it is a domestic crime: the interior minister cites the suspect's radical, possibly far-right views, police say he acted alone, and no official has named a foreign link, so any claim of a Russian hand runs ahead of the evidence. Zakharova's 'legitimate targets' line is a threat, but a repeat of a position Moscow stated in July, and it concerns troops in Ukraine rather than NATO territory; her claim that the KOALICJA drills aim at Russia's military defeat misrepresents an exercise built around deployment after hostilities end. Poland's Kaliningrad warning window reaches its scheduled end without a confirmed incident, which does not show the warnings were wrong. The Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November remain the main thing to watch for the baseline, since a ceasefire could in time free Russian forces. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland now treats the Kraków shooting as terrorism by a lone far-right attacker, and its digital-security institute reports a wave of false online claims about it, some pushed by Russia-linked accounts. Coalition of the Willing drills begin in Poland as Moscow repeats that foreign troops in Ukraine are unacceptable. No sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. ISW reports nothing significant in Belarus and says Russian losses have outpaced recruitment since July, and a leak of Russian state statistics points to very heavy war deaths. This fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new drone, border or GPS incident and no new sabotage case was first reported in the last day. The main hybrid activity was informational: Poland's NASK flagged more than 2,000 accounts, many automated and some with Russian markers, spreading false claims after the Kraków shooting, including a story, traced to a Russian Telegram channel, that the gunman fought for Ukraine. The wider pattern in the Lithuanian assessment (shadow-fleet risks, GPS interference around Kaliningrad, recruitment by hostile services) is unchanged.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged (17 of 39). Incident counts: official Russian threats fall from 1 to 0 (Zakharova's 8 November remarks repeat earlier positions without a new explicit threat); airspace incidents, sabotage cases, GPS jamming reports and border incidents stay at 0. New: Polish prosecutors treat the Kraków attack as terrorism with a far-right motive; a documented disinformation wave about it, partly Russia-linked; a Ukrainian intelligence claim that Russia recruits Ukrainian refugees for sabotage in Europe; ISW and leaked Rosstat data on Russian losses; a Ukrainian claim that Russia used the Oleshky truce to move in over 1,000 troops.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: the near-term conventional threat stays low, and the clearest new military data, ISW's finding that Russian losses have exceeded recruitment since July and a hacked Rosstat dataset suggesting over 400,000 war deaths, point to forces still absorbed by Ukraine, not freed up for the Baltic direction. The Kraków attack is now formally a terrorism case, but prosecutors and the interior minister describe a lone attacker with far-right views; nothing public supports either a Russian hand or the Russian-origin story that he was a Ukrainian fighter, which a fact-check rated false. What the case does show is the information-warfare pattern the baseline describes: within hours, bot networks, some with Russian markers, and some domestic political voices pushed conflicting false narratives; NASK's data show amplification, not who ordered it. Ukraine's foreign intelligence claim that Russia recruits Ukrainian refugees for sabotage fits court cases and Lithuania's recent expulsions, but its figures come from a party to the war and are not independently sourced. The Ukrainian claim that Russia used the Oleshky truce to reinforce is unverified, yet it is a useful warning for the Abu Dhabi talks on 10–11 November: a ceasefire is the main way Russian forces could, in time, be freed up. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: US-brokered talks with Russia and Ukraine open in Abu Dhabi, with Moscow again seeking a pullback of NATO forces from Eastern Europe and Poland warning against deals over its head. The Kraków gunman has died and prosecutors now say his motive is unclear. Finland's navy chief judges that Russia's Baltic presence has probably peaked. No sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. Finland's navy commander told Sky News that Russia's Baltic Sea presence has probably peaked for now, possibly because it has reached what it can sustain in peacetime. This fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new drone, border or GPS incident and no new sabotage case was first reported in the last day. Estonia's interior minister told the Financial Times that Russian attacks in Europe should be called state terrorism, not 'hybrid' incidents, and cyberattacks that overheated supermarket freezers in several European countries remain unattributed; Moscow denies a role. The information fight over the Kraków shooting continues, with analysts expecting more false claims before Poland's 11 November Independence March. The wider pattern in the Lithuanian assessment is unchanged.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged (17 of 39). All five incident counts stay at 0 (yesterday: 0 each). New: the Abu Dhabi talks opened on 10 November with security issues first on the agenda and Europeans present alongside but not at the table; in Kraków, prosecutors say the motive is not established and found no extremist symbols, so the far-right claim moves from Likely to Contested; Finland's navy chief says Russia's Baltic presence has probably peaked; Shoigu accused Poland and the Baltic states of expanding NATO infrastructure; Estonia's interior minister calls Russian sabotage state terrorism.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing public suggests Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or turned toward the Baltic direction, and the Finnish navy's judgement that Russia's Baltic presence has plateaued points the same way. The main question now is diplomatic. In Abu Dhabi, Moscow still demands that NATO pull back deployments in Central and Eastern Europe and rejects a general ceasefire, while US envoys talk of a wider European security arrangement; Poland's foreign minister warns against Western Europe dealing with Russia over Eastern Europe's head. A deal that limited allied forces on the eastern flank, or a ceasefire that let Russia rebuild, would matter more for the Baltic states than any single incident this week; neither has happened. On Kraków, coverage ran ahead of the evidence in both directions: the early official framing of a far-right attacker is now disputed by prosecutors, and there is still no public evidence of a Russian role, although Russia-linked accounts did amplify false stories. Estonia's 'state terrorism' framing and the freezer cyberattacks show how hybrid pressure is being described more sharply, but attribution for the freezer attacks rests on claims by pro-Russian hacker groups and researchers' judgement, not on official findings. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Drone alerts sweep all three Baltic states overnight as Ukraine strikes ports and a refinery in Russia's Leningrad region; Kaunas, Vilnius and Panevėžys areas told to shelter, and Finland restricts the eastern Gulf of Finland. A balloon-type object from Belarus briefly shut Vilnius and Kaunas airports. Abu Dhabi talks enter their final day. No sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. The overnight drone alerts are linked to Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russia's Baltic coast, not to Russian ground forces. This fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: The night of 10–11 November brought the widest wave of drone alerts in weeks: shelter warnings in Lithuania (including Kaunas and Panevėžys), across eastern and central Latvia and in southern and eastern Estonia, with NATO jets in the air and a drone that apparently crossed Lithuania into Latvia. Earlier that evening a balloon-type object from Belarus forced restrictions at Vilnius and Kaunas airports, which Lithuania calls part of Belarus's hybrid attack. Poland detained two Ukrainian citizens accused of spying and arson for Russian intelligence. The wider pattern in the Lithuanian assessment is unchanged.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score is unchanged (17 of 39), but airspace and border pressure are now rated Rising. Incident counts rose from all zeros yesterday: airspace incidents 2 (drones entering Lithuanian and Latvian airspace overnight), sabotage cases 1 (Poland's arrest of two men accused of arson and spying for Russia), border incidents 1 (the balloon-type object from Belarus that shut Vilnius and Kaunas airports); GPS reports and official Russian threats stay at 0. Also new: Finland's temporary air and sea restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Finland; Poland's justice minister says there are strong traces of right-wing extremism in the Kraków case, while prosecutors stay cautious; Belarus's foreign minister claims NATO keeps up to 30,000 troops in the Baltic region.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: the overnight drone alarms reflect Ukraine's strikes on Russian ports near the Estonian border and the jamming-heavy air space around them, not Russian forces moving toward the Baltic states. The origin of the drones that crossed into Lithuania and Latvia has not been officially established; earlier strays this year were mostly Ukrainian drones knocked off course, and Moscow's line that Kyiv uses NATO airspace as cover remains unsupported by evidence. The practical effect is still real: tens of thousands of residents were told to shelter and airports closed twice in one night, which is the kind of disruption the baseline describes. The Belarus balloon flights continue as a low-cost, deniable pressure tool. In Abu Dhabi, the talks are being described as constructive, but the Kremlin still rejects a European seat and a ceasefire, and reported territorial flexibility rests on one anonymous US official. Nothing yet suggests a deal that would limit allied forces on the eastern flank. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: New details on the night of 10–11 November: NATO jets twice failed to shoot down a drone that entered Lithuania from Belarus, and debris from one missile fell in a forest in Biržai district. Lithuania's army thinks it was probably a stray Ukrainian drone, but its origin is unconfirmed, and Poland does not confirm Lithuania's report that it briefly crossed into Polish airspace. Finland suspects a five-minute violation of its airspace the same night. US envoys meet Putin in Moscow today after the Abu Dhabi talks. Still no sign of Russian forces preparing a conventional attack.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. The CSTO summit in Moscow talked about strengthening joint air defence and drone defence but announced no deployments. This fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: The fallout from the 10–11 November drone night dominates: a failed NATO interception over Lithuania, a missile exploding over a rural area, a suspected Finnish airspace violation and a Russian-amplified disinformation push telling Lithuanians the warnings were pointless or that Vilnius lets Ukrainian drones through. Balloon smuggling from Belarus continues. No new sabotage arrest, GPS-jamming report or explicit Russian threat was found. The wider pattern in the Lithuanian assessment is unchanged.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score stays at 17 of 39; airspace and border pressure move from Rising back to Unchanged because no new incursion or border incident followed. Incident counts fall from 4 to 1: airspace incidents 1 (Finland's suspected drone violation over the eastern Gulf of Finland, first reported after yesterday's edition), sabotage cases 0 (was 1), border incidents 0 (was 1), GPS reports and official Russian threats stay at 0. New since yesterday: the failed NATO interception and missile debris in Biržai district; a Lithuania–Poland contradiction over whether the drone entered Polish airspace; Lithuania's plan to automate shelter access; Ukraine's claim that it also hit a Russian missile ship at Ust-Luga.
bottom_line: Today's evidence remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: the drone scare grew out of Ukraine's strikes on Russia's Baltic coast and the electronic warfare around them, not from Russian forces moving toward the Baltic states. The more important finding is about defence, not intent: allied jets could not stop a single slow drone over Lithuania, and an interceptor missile came down near homes, which exposes a gap that Russia or Belarus could exploit deliberately. The drone's origin is still not officially established; Lithuania's army leans toward a stray Ukrainian drone, while Russian state media present that as fact and mock NATO. Lithuania's account that the drone touched Polish airspace is not confirmed by Poland, a reminder that early official statements can differ. Moscow's claim that the Baltic states let Ukrainian drones through is contradicted by the attempts to shoot this one down. In diplomacy, the Kremlin is using the talks to revive its 2021 demands on NATO's presence in the east, which is the point where any deal could directly affect Baltic security. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

The US says Europeans will join the next round of talks, but the Kremlin has not confirmed it. Finland's military says it detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland. Poland indicts a man over the 2025 rail sabotage and calls an FSB spy-ring claim disinformation. Still no sign of Russian forces preparing an attack on the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced near them. Finland's confirmation of a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland shows the Baltic Fleet is under Ukrainian pressure, not being freed up. This fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new drone incursion, GPS-jamming report or border provocation was found for the last two nights. The pressure has shifted to the information and diplomatic fields: the FSB says it broke up a Polish spy network in Kaliningrad, which Poland calls a staged provocation, and Moscow offers bilateral deals to individual NATO states. Poland's new indictment in the 2025 rail sabotage case is a reminder that Russian intelligence uses hired proxies. The wider pattern described in the Lithuanian assessment is unchanged.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score stays at 17 of 39; airspace moves from Unchanged to Easing after two nights without new incursions. New since yesterday: the Russian proposal of bilateral non-aggression pacts with NATO states and the Baltic and EU rejection of Russia's 'security architecture' agenda; a US–Kremlin difference over whether Europeans will join the talks; Finland's confirmation of a strike on a Russian warship; the FSB's Kaliningrad spy claim and Poland's rebuttal; a RAND Europe scenario of a 2030 Russian attack on Estonia.
bottom_line: Today's evidence remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing points to Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states, and Finland's statement suggests the Baltic Fleet is itself coming under Ukrainian attack. The sharper Baltic risk this week is diplomatic. Moscow is trying to make a new European 'security architecture', including limits on NATO forces in the east, part of any Ukraine settlement, and its offer of separate non-aggression pacts with individual NATO members reads as an attempt to split the alliance rather than to add security; Baltic leaders and the EU have rejected both, and the US has not endorsed them. Coverage runs ahead of the evidence on two points: the US says Europeans will join the next round, but the Kremlin has not confirmed it, and the FSB's Kaliningrad spy claim rests only on Russian material that Polish officials and fact-checkers say looks staged. Poland's sabotage indictment concerns a 2025 attack, not a new one. The RAND Europe war scenario is an exercise, not a forecast, though it matches the baseline's longer-term warning. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: A German tabloid, Bild, reports that Russian envoys floated a plan in Abu Dhabi under which Finland would leave NATO and no NATO bases would be allowed in Estonia, Latvia or Lithuania; the Kremlin denies raising Finland, and Finland calls such ideas outrageous and not negotiable. Moscow also sets conditions for European participation in the next round of talks, contradicting the US account. No new drone incursion, GPS-jamming report, border provocation or sabotage case was found, and there is still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced. The war at sea is running the other way: Russia has still not commented on the reported Ukrainian strike on one of its missile ships in the Gulf of Finland. This fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: A third night without new drone incursions, and no new GPS-jamming, border or sabotage reports. The pressure is now mainly political and informational: reported Russian proposals to keep NATO bases out of the Baltic states, Russian narratives casting Europe as the obstacle to peace, and a Polish security firm's warning that the 16 November anniversary of the 2025 rail sabotage could be used for new disinformation. The wider pattern described in the Lithuanian assessment is unchanged.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score stays at 17 of 39. Incident counts fall from 1 to 0: sabotage cases 0 (was 1), and airspace incidents, GPS reports, border incidents and official Russian threats all stay at 0. New since yesterday: Bild's report of informal Russian proposals that include Finland leaving NATO and a ban on NATO bases in the Baltic states, the Kremlin's partial denial and Finland's rejection; the Kremlin's condition that Europe must first show it will 'contribute' before joining talks, contradicting US envoys; Putin's warning, reported by Kyiv Post, that European troops in Ukraine after a deal would be legitimate targets (a repeat of earlier warnings, not a new threat to NATO territory).
bottom_line: Today's evidence remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing points to Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states, and the military indicators are as quiet as yesterday. The main news is a leak, not a deed. Bild's report fits a pattern that is now well established from on-the-record sources, including Russia's own negotiator and Lithuanian, Finnish and EU leaders: Moscow wants Ukraine talks to cover limits on NATO in the east. But the specific demands, Finland leaving NATO and no NATO bases in the Baltic states, rest on anonymous sources, Bild itself says it is one of several informal proposals, and the Kremlin denies the Finland part, so they should be treated as unconfirmed. Coverage is running ahead of the evidence: many outlets present Bild's list as Putin's demands, but they all trace back to one report. The two sides also tell different stories about whether Europeans will join the next round. Whatever the exact wording, any such demand would hit the core of the Baltic states' security, and Baltic, Finnish and EU leaders have rejected it. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: A leaked Russian paper, reported by The New York Times and The Telegraph, asks NATO to pull its forces back to where they stood in 1997, which would mean leaving Poland, the Baltic states and Finland, and asks Britain and France not to use their nuclear weapons to protect other European allies. Estonia's military says the Russian missile ship hit in the Gulf of Finland suffered casualties and had to be escorted home. A fourth night passed without drone incursions, and there is still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced. Estonia's military now confirms that Ukrainian drones damaged the Baltic Fleet corvette Naro-Fominsk, with dead and wounded, so the fleet is being worn down rather than freed up. This fits Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: A fourth night without new drone incursions, and no new GPS-jamming, border or sabotage reports. Poland plans to extend its closed zone on the Belarus border for 90 days, citing persistent migrant pressure and more balloons and drones flying in from Belarus. Tomorrow, 16 November, is the anniversary of the 2025 Polish rail sabotage, which analysts expect to be used for disinformation. The pressure remains mainly political and informational, as described in the Lithuanian assessment.
changed: No change in indicator ratings, so the threat score stays at 17 of 39, and incident counts stay at 0 in all five categories. New since yesterday: The New York Times and The Telegraph describe a Russian paper dated 10 November that demands a NATO pull-back to 1997 positions and limits on British and French nuclear protection of Europe, turning what was earlier an anonymous-source expectation into a reported written demand; the accounts of that paper do not include Bild's point about Finland leaving NATO; Estonia's military gave new details of the Gulf of Finland strike (several drone hits, casualties, ship escorted home); US Senate intelligence chair Tom Cotton called the 1997 demand preposterous; Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman said Europe would be safer without NATO; Poland plans to extend its Belarus border zone.
bottom_line: Today's evidence remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing points to Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states, and the Baltic Fleet has just lost a missile ship to damage. The main development is on paper, not on the ground. Two major outlets now describe a written Russian position, dated 10 November and seen by The New York Times through a negotiator and confirmed by a second source, that would push NATO out of every state that joined after 1997, including all three Baltic states. That makes the broad demand, earlier reported only through anonymous expectations, much better supported, though the paper is unsigned, has not been published and the Kremlin has not commented on it. Bild's narrower claim that Moscow asked Finland to leave NATO is not in those accounts and stays contested. Coverage tends to call this an ultimatum, but it is an opening negotiating position that the US, Finland, the Baltic states and European leaders reject; its significance is that Moscow still frames peace in Ukraine as a rollback of Baltic security, as the baseline judges. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Estonia says Russia's military intelligence (GRU) ordered a foiled arson attack on the drone maker Threod Systems near Tallinn; eight residents of Latvia were detained, and Estonia will close its road border crossings with Russia on 1 December. Moscow calls the closure Russophobia, and the Kremlin says talks on European security are pointless if Europe does not want peace. Still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced; ISW again reports nothing significant on Belarus. The Baltic Fleet is still absorbing the loss of a damaged missile ship. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: A new sabotage attempt: on 14 November security staff stopped an attempt to set fire to Threod Systems, which makes reconnaissance and attack drones, in Viimsi near Tallinn. Estonia's security police (KAPO) says the GRU coordinated it; Latvia's security service (VDD) tipped Estonia off and found explosives in Latvia. It is the second arson attempt on an Estonian defence firm since August, and exactly the kind of proxy sabotage the Lithuanian assessment warns about. No new drone incursions, GPS-jamming reports or border provocations.
changed: Indicator ratings are unchanged, so the threat score stays at 17 of 39; the sabotage indicator stays High but its trend is now Rising. Incident counts rise from 0 to 1 in total: sabotage cases 1 (was 0: the foiled GRU-linked arson at Threod Systems); airspace incidents, GPS reports, border incidents and official Russian threats stay at 0. Also new: Estonia will close its Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula road crossings on 1 December; Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman called this Russophobia; the Kremlin spokesman said Russia would have to use force to reach its goals if no deal with Europe is possible; drones hit four commercial ships in Romanian waters, one of them Greek-flagged, according to ISW.
bottom_line: Today's evidence remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing points to Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states, and the main threat is still hybrid. The Threod case is well supported: an attack was physically stopped, eight people were detained, explosives were seized in Latvia, and two national security services, Estonia's and Latvia's, independently point to Russia. The GRU attribution itself rests on intelligence that has not been made public, so it is a strong official judgement rather than proven fact, and Russia has not yet answered this specific accusation. Estonia's decision to close its road crossings is a defensive political response to sabotage, not a military signal, although Moscow is already framing it as hostility toward Russians. The Kremlin's remark that Russia would have to use force if Europe does not want peace is vague and refers to its war aims; some coverage presents it as a threat to Europe, which goes further than the words. The pattern of hired local proxies, recruited online, matches what VSD described in its 2026 assessment. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

No new incidents were counted, and there is still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders, and no new Russian or Belarusian exercise announced. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new sabotage case, drone incursion, Baltic GPS-jamming report or border provocation was first reported since yesterday, but the fallout from the foiled GRU-linked arson at Threod Systems in Estonia continues: Moscow denies any role, Estonia is closing its road crossings with Russia on 1 December, and Lithuania says it could follow. changed: The threat score is unchanged at 17 of 39; the only rating change is the sabotage trend, back from Rising to Unchanged because no new case was reported. New since yesterday: the Kremlin called Estonia's accusation entirely baseless; Lithuania's president said Lithuania may also consider closing its border with Russia; two US Army battalions arrived in Lithuania, which has also proposed a permanent US base; the EU added 113 sanctions listings and revealed that its naval mission boarded a falsely flagged suspected shadow-fleet tanker in the Mediterranean on 13 November.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing points to Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states, and the pressure remains hybrid and political. The contradiction worth watching is over the Threod case: Estonia's security police, prosecutors and foreign minister say they have clear evidence that the GRU ordered the attack, while the Kremlin calls this entirely baseless; neither side has published its evidence, but the Estonian account rests on detentions, seized materials and a separate Latvian investigation, while the Russian denial offers no alternative explanation. The diplomatic consequences are growing faster than the facts: Lithuania openly weighing a border closure would be a significant step because of Kaliningrad transit, but for now it is a conditional statement, not a decision. Some coverage frames Estonia's plans to keep state services running from abroad as preparation for imminent invasion; it is contingency planning that Estonia has pursued for years. The arrival of US battalions is a deterrence measure on the allied side, not a reaction to any new Russian move. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Estonia's president says closing the Russian border must not be an emotional decision, and the cabinet has yet to formally decide its length; Lavrov restates Moscow's 2021 demands on NATO. No new incidents in the Baltic region for a second day, and still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.

Belarus announced a snap combat-readiness check of its border-guard rapid-response units on 16 November, without saying where; it is a border-guard drill, not an army exercise, and ISW found nothing significant in Belarus on 17 November. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new sabotage case, drone incursion, Baltic GPS-jamming report or border provocation was first reported since yesterday. bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing points to Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states, and the pressure remains hybrid and political. The visible disagreement today is inside Estonia, not between Estonia and Russia: the foreign minister announced a closure from 1 December, the prime minister wants it indefinite, and the president questions whether it fits the threat, since the Threod suspects were residents of Latvia recruited at a distance. That is a normal policy debate about means, not doubt about who is behind the attacks, but Russian outlets are likely to present it as a split. Lavrov's statement that Moscow still holds to its 2021 demands matches the leaked paper on pulling NATO back and shows the Kremlin's long-term aims toward the Baltic region, but it is diplomatic positioning, not a sign of military preparation. Belarus's snap inspection of border units may be reported as escalation; it is a routine type of drill with no reported movement toward NATO borders. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: A Polish newspaper reports that Russia planned a mass-casualty false-flag attack near the Kaliningrad border to blame on Ukraine; Warsaw neither confirms nor denies it. Russia is also reported to be offering to thin its forces in Kaliningrad and Belarus if NATO pulls back to its 1997 footprint. Still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Ukraine's military intelligence said on 18 November that a direct attack on the Baltic states or Poland is unlikely while Russia's ground forces are tied up in Ukraine, although it says Russia is adding ammunition and fuel depots in Kaliningrad, Belarus and western Russia; that claim has not been shown with imagery. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat, with long-term rebuilding.
hybrid_note: No new sabotage case, drone incursion, Baltic GPS-jamming report or border provocation was first reported since yesterday, the eighth day without a drone incursion in the region. The threat picture stays high: Rzeczpospolita reports, citing anonymous senior sources, that Russian intelligence planned a sabotage attack with mass casualties near the Polish–Kaliningrad border in late October or early November, to be blamed on Ukraine, and that the Baltic states received similar warnings. This is the provocation and proxy-sabotage pattern the Lithuanian assessment describes.
changed: The threat score is unchanged at 17 of 39, with no rating changes, and all five incident counts stay at 0. New since yesterday: Rzeczpospolita's anonymous-source report of a foiled Russian false-flag plot near the Kaliningrad border, with Poland's special-services minister saying only that the threat was judged real; Bloomberg and the New York Times report that Russia's negotiating paper offers to reduce forces in Kaliningrad and Belarus in return for a NATO rollback to 1997; Ukraine's military intelligence called a direct attack on the Baltic states or Poland unlikely but said Russia is building depots near NATO borders; Estonia's parliament backed a border-closure bill in first reading, 37 to 2. Catching up: Lithuania extended army patrols on the Kaliningrad border to the end of November.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: nothing shows Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states, and even Ukraine's military intelligence, which has reason to stress the Russian threat, calls a direct attack unlikely for now. The false-flag story is serious if true, but it rests on anonymous sources; Poland's government neither confirms nor denies it, and the versions already differ, with the Polish paper describing an attack on Polish territory and The Telegraph's retelling describing Russian civilians as the victims. Treat it as a plausible but unconfirmed account of the early-November border alert that Tusk announced at the time. The reported Russian offer to thin forces in Kaliningrad and Belarus is a bargaining position tied to the old demand that NATO leave the states that joined after 1997; headlines that say Russia would pull its troops out of Kaliningrad go further than the reporting, which says it is unclear what a reduction would mean. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Lithuania presents a plan to put fencing on parts of its border with Kaliningrad, while officials stress the threat level there has not risen. A Russian envoy warns of a response from Russia's strategic forces if Lithuania and Poland lift their bans on hosting nuclear weapons. Still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Lithuanian officials presenting the Kaliningrad border plan on 19 November said the threat level at that border has not risen. Ukraine's military intelligence repeated that Russia is strengthening logistics near NATO borders and in Belarus, without imagery or locations. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat, with long-term rebuilding.
hybrid_note: No new sabotage case, drone incursion, Baltic GPS-jamming report or border provocation was first reported since yesterday, the ninth day without a drone incursion in the region. The threat picture stays high because of recent GRU-linked sabotage attempts, including the foiled arson at an Estonian drone maker on 14 November, persistent navigation interference from the Kaliningrad area and the still-unconfirmed report of a planned false-flag attack near the Polish–Kaliningrad border. Catching up on 18 November items missed yesterday: Russia's envoy at the OSCE security forum warned of 'response measures' by its strategic deterrence forces if Lithuania and Poland lift nuclear-weapons bans, and Ukraine's foreign ministry said Russia is building an information pretext for possible aggression against NATO's eastern flank.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: the new items are political signals, defensive measures and warnings, not signs that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic states. Lithuania's fencing plan is a precaution against hybrid incidents and draft evaders, and its own officials say the threat at the border has not risen, so it should not be read as evidence of an imminent Russian move. The Russian envoy's warning about nuclear response measures is conditional and tied to Lithuania's ongoing constitutional debate; her claim that NATO is assessing nuclear deployments in Lithuania and Poland is not backed by any NATO decision. Ukraine's foreign ministry warns of pretext-building against NATO, while Ukraine's military intelligence said a day earlier that a direct attack is unlikely for now; the two fit together only if the warning is read as being about information operations and longer-term risk, not an imminent attack. The false-flag story has still not been confirmed by any government. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Two Russian missiles, one of them a Kh-101 cruise missile, and a jet-powered drone came down in eastern Poland during a large Russian strike on Ukraine. Poland calls it an intentional provocation and NATO a grave violation; no one was hurt. Russia vows a response to Estonia's border closure. Still no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. The objects that fell in Poland were part of a strike on Ukraine, not a military move against NATO. ISW again reported nothing significant on Belarus on 19 November. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine, with long-term rebuilding.
hybrid_note: The airspace picture worsened: Poland says three Russian objects crossed into its airspace overnight into 20 November and landed near Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz, ending a nine-day lull in airspace incidents in the region. The 14 November GRU-linked arson attempt in Estonia and persistent navigation interference from the Kaliningrad area keep the hybrid level high, as the Lithuanian assessment describes.

Airspace incidents rise from 0 to 3 and official Russian threats from 0 to 1 (Zakharova's pledge of political and diplomatic retaliation if Estonia closes its border). Also new: Estonia's government formally approved closing all five road crossings with Russia from 1 December; Poland will ask NATO for more support on the eastern flank; Trump said hours before the incident that Putin had sent drones and 'little missiles' into Poland by mistake, while Tusk said this does not look like an accident.
bottom_line: The missile landings in Poland are the most serious airspace incident in weeks, but the evidence so far points to spillover from a massive strike on western Ukraine rather than an attack on Poland: no damage or casualties, and the impact sites lie roughly 30–60 km from the Ukrainian border. Poland's claim that the timing was deliberate, near a Coalition of the Willing exercise, is a judgement that no published evidence yet proves or disproves; early reports also differed on whether two or three objects were involved, which Poland's defence minister has since settled at three. Trump's description of past incursions as mistakes and Tusk's view that this was intentional are the clearest contradiction of the day, and Russia has not yet commented. Zakharova's warning to Estonia is limited to political and diplomatic measures and does not change the military picture. Overall today's evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: hybrid pressure and risky behaviour near NATO borders, no sign that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or moved toward the Baltic states. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.
