Airspace incidents fall from 3 to 0 and official Russian threats from 1 to 0; the other counts stay at 0. New: drones struck the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which serves Russia's defence ministry, in the Gulf of Finland on 21 November; NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte visited Warsaw and Poland asked for more air defence and surveillance aircraft but not for Article 4 consultations; the Kremlin denied any airspace violation; unverified explosions and air alerts were reported around Baltiysk in Kaliningrad.
bottom_line: The day's most important event happened at sea, not on a NATO border: a Russian defence-logistics ship was hit by drones in the Gulf of Finland, and the Finnish military's view that Ukraine is quite possibly responsible is a judgement, not a confirmed attribution; Ukraine has not commented. The incident matters for the Baltic states because the Kaliningrad supply route now runs through an active risk zone, and the official accounts of where the strike happened already differ (Russia says neutral waters near its border, Estonia an international lane north of Vaindloo, Finland international waters before the ship drifted into Finnish territory). On Poland, the facts remain clear and the intent unclear: Polish officials, NATO and ISW read deliberate testing, the Kremlin denies any violation, and Russian state media present the foreign minister's call to wait for confirmed facts as an admission that there is no proof, which it is not. Moscow's line that it has no plan to attack NATO, given alongside claims that NATO seeks war, is familiar messaging rather than a change of course. Overall the evidence is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: high hybrid risk around the Baltic Sea, no sign that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Polish prosecutors say all three objects that crossed into Poland on 20 November were Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles, and NATO ambassadors meet in Brussels today at Poland's call. The burning Russian ship Sparta II has been towed out of Finnish waters. Russian outlets now blame NATO, Poland and Lithuania for Saturday's Kaliningrad alert; Warsaw and Vilnius call this false. No sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. The missiles in Poland strayed from a mass strike on Ukraine, and the Gulf of Finland ship strike is part of the Russia–Ukraine war spilling into the Baltic Sea, not a Russian military move against NATO. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new airspace violation, sabotage case, Baltic GPS-jamming report, border provocation or explicit Russian threat was first reported since yesterday. The information space is the busiest front: Poland's counter-disinformation centre flagged a wave of Russian claims that NATO, Poland, Lithuania or German troops were behind the Kaliningrad alert. Together with last week's missile landings, the GRU-linked arson attempt in Estonia and persistent navigation interference, this keeps hybrid risk high, as the Lithuanian baseline describes.
changed: The threat score is unchanged at 18 of 39 with no rating changes, and all five counts stay at 0. New: Lublin prosecutors said on 22 November that all three objects were Kh-101 missiles made recently in Dubna near Moscow (Poland first spoke of two missiles and a drone); the North Atlantic Council holds an extraordinary meeting on 23 November; the Sparta II was towed out of Finland's economic zone on 22 November; Poland's commander of operations confirmed on the record that a Swedish Gripen had clearance to fire but could not identify the missile in bad weather; Russian outlets began blaming NATO, Poland and Lithuania for the Kaliningrad alert. Correction: our 22 November edition missed that Finland's defence ministry on 21 November reported a suspected Russian helicopter airspace violation off Loviisa during the ship rescue; it is still under investigation and is noted, not counted, today.
bottom_line: The facts about Poland are firmer today: prosecutors' preliminary findings say three Russian Kh-101 missiles came down, which replaces the earlier two-missiles-and-a-drone account, though one specialist outlet still reports doubt about the other two objects until the last site is examined. Whether the incursion was deliberate remains a judgement: Polish leaders suggest a provocation timed to an allied exercise, but no flight-path evidence has been published, and Moscow still denies any violation. The Kaliningrad story shows coverage running well ahead of evidence on both sides: Ukrainian channels and some headlines spoke of a strike on the Baltic Fleet base, yet no damage has been verified and a viral photo came from Iran, while Russian outlets turned an unexplained alert into accusations against NATO, Poland and Lithuania that rest on nothing published. Finland's suspected helicopter violation looks linked to the rescue, not to a probe of Finnish defences, but the investigation is open. Overall the picture is consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: high hybrid and information pressure around the Baltic Sea, and no sign that Russian forces are being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Russia's foreign ministry says Estonia is on the verge of triggering open war, after Tallinn decided to close its road crossings with Russia from 1 December. NATO ambassadors met on the Russian missiles that fell in Poland, but no decisions have been published. Lithuania calls Russia's Kaliningrad accusations a psychological operation. No sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Russia's plan for two rail ferries to Kaliningrad, due by 2030, is a long-term supply measure, not a sign of imminent military action. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: The sharpest new item is rhetorical: on 23 November Russia's foreign ministry summoned Estonia's chargé d'affaires and said Tallinn's actions were bringing the situation close to open war. No new airspace violation, sabotage case, Baltic GPS-jamming report or border provocation was first reported. Prosecutors from Poland, Germany, Lithuania and Bulgaria plan a joint team on the Starlink arson attacks, and Ukraine's military intelligence says Russia recruits saboteurs through job ads on messaging apps. Hybrid risk stays high, as the Lithuanian baseline describes.
changed: The threat score is unchanged at 18 of 39. 'Official Russian rhetoric' stays Elevated but its trend moves from Unchanged to Rising, and the 'Official Russian threats' count rises from 0 to 1 (the foreign ministry's open-war warning to Estonia); the other four counts stay at 0. New: the North Atlantic Council met on 23 November without a published outcome, and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said it was for the authorities to establish whether the missile incursion was deliberate; Poland's defence minister said allied early-warning aircraft were reinforcing Polish airspace; Russia announced two rail ferries for Kaliningrad; four EU states plan a joint Starlink arson investigation; a media-monitoring analysis found most 'NATO attack' posts about Kaliningrad came from three accounts.
bottom_line: Moscow's warning to Estonia is the strongest official Russian language toward a Baltic state in this briefing so far, but it came as a diplomatic protest with only political and diplomatic countermeasures reserved, not with any reported military step. Its accusations, that Estonia lets Ukrainian drones use its airspace and falsely blamed Russia for the arson attempt at a drone maker, rest on no published evidence, and Estonia denies them. On Poland, the facts have not moved since prosecutors identified three Kh-101 missiles; NATO has not published what the council agreed, and early reports differ on whether the early-warning aircraft are already flying or still coming. Some coverage runs ahead of the evidence: Ukrainian headlines present Russia's Kaliningrad ferries as preparation for a NATO blockade, yet NATO has announced no such plan and the ferries are due only by 2030; a German tabloid's claim that tanks went to Lithuania by rail to avoid provoking Moscow rests on unnamed sources and Berlin calls the routing routine. Overall the picture remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: heavy hybrid and information pressure, including nuclear-free but escalating rhetoric, and no sign of Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland reports a second Russian incursion: a jet-powered drone flew about 20 km into its airspace on the night of 23–24 November before turning back, and NATO is sending an AWACS surveillance aircraft. Sweden warns pilots of possible GPS jamming around Stockholm until the end of the year. Estonia's prime minister calls the coming border closure indefinite in substance. No sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders. Finland's parliamentary defence committee chair backs building anti-tank barriers on the Russian border, a long-term precaution rather than a response to a new threat. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: Two new items: a Russian jet-powered drone entered Polish airspace from Ukraine for about nine minutes on the night of 23–24 November, and Swedish aviation authorities issued a warning of possible GPS jamming and spoofing within about 175 km of Stockholm, valid until 31 December, after flight data showed a sharp rise in interference. The origin of the Swedish interference is not established. No new sabotage case, border provocation or explicit Russian threat was first reported. Hybrid risk stays high, as the Lithuanian baseline describes.
changed: The threat score is unchanged at 18 of 39. 'Airspace violations and drones' and 'GPS jamming and spoofing' stay High but their trends move from Unchanged to Rising; 'Official Russian rhetoric' stays Elevated and its trend returns from Rising to Unchanged. Counts: airspace incidents rise from 0 to 1 (the drone over Poland), GPS jamming reports from 0 to 1 (Stockholm), official Russian threats fall from 1 to 0; sabotage and border incidents stay at 0. New: NATO's military commander authorised forward deployment of an AWACS aircraft to Poland; Poland renewed its request for permanent US troops; Poland's operational commander said a NATO fighter had conditional clearance to fire on 20 November but held fire in bad weather; Estonia's prime minister said closing the Narva rail crossing could be the next step.
bottom_line: The new facts are on NATO's side of the border: Poland has now recorded a second Russian object in four days, and NATO has answered with more surveillance (an AWACS aircraft) rather than any offensive step, which Polish officials stress themselves. Warsaw says the drone was sent deliberately, but this is an assessment, not a published finding; detailed flight data so far come from unnamed sources quoted by RMF24, and Moscow has not commented. The Stockholm GPS story is real at the level of the official aviation warning, but claims that it comes from Russia run ahead of the evidence: Sweden's Transport Agency says the source is unknown. Lithuanian officials themselves read the Kaliningrad episode differently, with the defence minister calling it a provocation attempt and the president's security adviser seeing Russian fear of Ukrainian strikes; both reject any Lithuanian role. Overall the picture remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: sustained hybrid pressure along NATO's eastern edge and no sign of Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.

headline: Poland will seek a no-fly zone along its eastern border after last week's missile and drone incursions. Lithuanian prosecutors detained five people suspected of paid work for Russian state media and charged a man with spying on aid to Ukraine. Latvia's prime minister says Estonia closed its Russia border in haste. No new incursion, jamming report or explicit Russian threat, and no sign of Russian forces preparing to attack the Baltic states.
conventional_note: No reports of Russian troops massing, field hospitals, blood supplies or equipment trains moving toward Baltic borders; ISW reports nothing significant in Belarus. Estonian analyst Ilmar Raag argues Russia lacks the resources for a second front. This matches Lithuania's 2026 National Threat Assessment: a low near-term conventional threat while most Russian forces are tied up in Ukraine.
hybrid_note: No new airspace incursion, sabotage case, GPS jamming report or border provocation was first reported since yesterday. New in the hybrid picture are two Lithuanian cases from 25 November: five people detained on suspicion of paid cooperation with Russian state broadcaster RTRS, and an indictment of a Lithuanian man accused of gathering intelligence for Russia on strategic infrastructure and aid to Ukraine. These are influence and espionage cases, not sabotage. Hybrid risk stays high, as the Lithuanian baseline describes.
changed: The threat score is unchanged at 18 of 39. No status changed; the trends for 'Airspace violations and drones' and 'GPS jamming and spoofing' return from Rising to Unchanged because no new incident was reported. Counts: airspace incidents fall from 1 to 0 and GPS jamming reports from 1 to 0; sabotage cases, border incidents and official Russian threats stay at 0. New: Poland's plan for a no-fly zone 12 to a few dozen km deep along its eastern border; the Lithuanian detentions and spy indictment; Latvia's prime minister criticising Estonia's border closure as rushed, with Riga due to decide on its own closure; Estonia's defence minister telling parliament that Ukraine does not use Estonian airspace to attack Russia.
bottom_line: Today's evidence is about NATO states tightening their defences and their counter-intelligence, not about Russian military moves: Poland's planned no-fly zone and Lithuania's two prosecutions are responses to pressure already reported. The Lithuanian cases are allegations at the suspicion and indictment stage, and should not be read as proven. The clearest new disagreement is inside the Baltic camp: Latvia's prime minister says Estonia should have consulted its neighbours and acted with elections in mind, while Tallinn points to twelve attacks it attributes to Russia; this is a dispute over tactics, not over the threat. On the information side, Moscow's claim that Estonia lets Ukrainian drones use its airspace is now echoed by an Estonian MP, but the defence minister denies it and no flight data have been offered; a Debunk.org study shows the Baltic-complicity narrative has run in thousands of Kremlin-aligned articles since March. Overall the picture remains consistent with the Lithuanian baseline: sustained hybrid pressure and no sign of Russian forces being freed from Ukraine or redirected toward the Baltic states. Quiet logistics and medical indicators reflect a lack of public reporting, not proof that nothing is happening.
